events.what: request A is admitted and takes a token
burst request C is admitted; the bucket is empty
burst request D finds no token and is refused with a 429
first drop lands as a token
second drop lands as a token
request E is admitted with a refilled token
another drop lands as the view pulls back

skills.why: The owning workflow's Plan stage (§4–5 step 1): viewer arc, rhythm and duration driver
The value-first order of the scene and the rhythm of the moments: spend, burst, refusal, held refill, release
Accent discipline, readable mono labels for exact values, and narration pacing (about 2.5 words per second)
Revealing each piece on its spoken cue, and using a deliberate held window for the refill, without turning windows into cuts
One dominant motion idea (tokens leaving and returning), with motion verbs chosen per element

The source of the named recipes: card-morph-anchor, spring-pop-entrance, stat-bars-and-fills, svg-icon-enrichment, vertical-spring-ticker, viewport-change, the zoom-out-workspace-reveal blueprint and the MotionPath technique

moments.title: One request, one token

recipes.purpose: The request travels one fixed route: in from the user, past the bucket, out to the API
The top token detaches from the bucket, rises to meet the request and rides with it as one unit. No catalogued recipe covers this attach move, so construction builds it
The token counter beside the bucket rolls one digit per change, so the count is always readable

moments.title: A burst drains it

camera.subject: the bucket

moments.title: Refused

camera.reason: Keeping the frame still makes the stop and recoil read as the bucket's decision, not a cut
camera.subject: the bucket rim where D stops

moments.purpose: Make the rejection follow visibly from the empty bucket, and tie it to the 429 the request rate limiter returns.

narration.job: State the rejection rule as it happens

moments.title: Hold on the refill

The counter rolls 0 → 1 → 2

content.question: How is a per-user limit actually enforced?
content.takeaway: Each request spends one token from its user's bucket; a burst empties it, the next request is refused, and the bucket refills at a steady rate. Every user's bucket lives centrally, in Redis.

continuity.exit: Pulled back on the Redis store: a row of per-user buckets, ours holding 2 of 3 tokens with its drip still running
continuity.entry: A dark, empty stage holding only the request rate limiter's small bucket glyph

outgoing.note: Scene s06 (launch limiters safely) could open on this Redis store, since its first practice, failing open, is about what happens when the limiter or Redis breaks. This stays provisional until s06 has a reviewed plan.

treatments.text: Few, exact labels: the term in m1, a mono token counter that always equals the ledger, the 429 badge, the refill-rate label with N, and the Redis label. Narration does not appear as on-screen text. Labels use body type from the theme fallbacks; the counter and rate use mono.
treatments.camera: The camera holds for m1–m6 so every event plays out in one stable space, and pulls back once in m7 to reveal Redis. There is no zoom-in anywhere.
treatments.presenter: Undecided. The mechanism needs the full frame from m2 to m6, so any presenter would suit a short appearance at the open (m1) or beside the wide Redis view (m7), not during the demonstration.

unresolved: The draft narration is reordered to follow the creator's direction: 'and fresh tokens drip back in slowly.' moves after the refusal and the silent refill, spoken as 'Fresh tokens drip back in slowly.' Line 4 still says 'faster than the drip' before the drip is named; the visibly forming drop carries it, but the creator may prefer to reword it.

The source does not map the drip rate to N or the bucket size to the burst allowance. The 'refill: N tokens / second' label follows the standard reading of a token bucket, and the creator should confirm it.
The source does not name 429 for the token bucket. The 429 on request D follows the creator's request-rate script (cr-429).
The estimate of about 24 s is above an even share of the 120 s target across seven scenes (about 17 s). The silent hold in m5 and the pull-back in m7 are the places to trim once audio exists.
Voice source and presenter visibility are undecided. A soft, even tick as each drop lands could make the refill rhythm audible; no audio is planned until delivery is decided.

The user (cast-4e8f7fd4476d20bcfb21), request-rate-limiter (cast-be8d129feaa5af3270de) and HTTP 429 (cast-c637a420e8125820e51c) library objects were chosen from their library descriptions only; their artwork was not viewed in this run. Construction should confirm they read at this scale.
token-hand-off and refusal-recoil are adapted recipes that no catalogue entry covers. Every catalogued recipe named here is still unproven in the installed runtime.
content.development: Open the request rate limiter the viewer already knows and show that inside it is one user's bucket of tokens. Follow one calm request as it spends a token. Then a burst takes the rest before any refill lands, and the next request is turned back with a 429. Stay still while the bucket refills drop by drop, so the viewer feels the rate before the narration names it. Then name the rate as the limiter's N per second and let the next request through. Finally pull back once to show this bucket is one of many, all held in Redis. The whole scene is one continuous space: the camera holds until a single zoom-out at the end.

demonstration.text: One user's bucket holds 3 tokens. Request A takes one. A burst of B, C and D arrives before any refill lands: B and C take the last two and D is refused with a 429. During a held beat, two drops refill the bucket. Request E is admitted, and one more drop lands as the view pulls back to Redis. The refill is shown as N tokens per second, the same N as the request rate limiter's cap.
